sections.html:
Your choices in Madison are an agent listing, a private sale, or an as-is cash offer. After a contract is signed, the same three documents follow every route: the state transfer return, your condition report and the recorded deed. How fast you close depends largely on how little work the house needs first.

Renters make up much of Madison. Owners live in only 46.0% of homes, so many sellers are landlords or heirs with a unit that is leased or empty. Tenants, an unfinished permit or a short-term rental permit each bring extra steps that an ordinary owner-occupied sale avoids.

Use these citywide figures to see whether an offer is in a sensible range before you request comparable sales. A given street may run well above or below them.

sections.h2: Local details that affect a sale
sections.html:
Downtown stands on an isthmus between Lake Mendota and Lake Monona, and Madison curls around the separate municipalities of Maple Bluff, Monona and Shorewood Hills while also touching Sun Prairie, Middleton, McFarland and Fitchburg. Since Madison recently took in most of the remaining Town of Madison, look at the municipality named on your tax bill before deciding which rules apply.

The city officially recognizes over 120 neighborhood associations. On the near east side, Marquette holds the Marquette Bungalows Historic District and the Orton Park Historic District, and buyers also search by names such as Dudgeon-Monroe, near Lake Wingra, and Hilldale. Check with the city to see whether a historic district reaches your block.

sections.h2: What if the Madison house has been a short-term rental?
sections.html:
A buyer cannot take over your permit. The ZTRHP permit is issued to one host for one dwelling unit and cannot be transferred. Guests staying fewer than 30 nights make a rental short-term in the city's eyes, and state law calls the arrangement a tourist rooming house. Airbnb or VRBO listings should be closed, and the buyer should know the permit ends with you.

Rules for permit holders:

  • The unit has to be the host's primary dwelling during the rental and for the 12 consecutive months before it began.
  • While the host is away, the rental can run no more than 30 days per licensing year, July 1 to June 30.
  • Guest limits are the smaller of twice the legal bedrooms or 12 people, with children under 12 not counted.
  • A $300 one-time application fee applies, and renewal costs $100 a year.
  • Violations bring fines of $500 to $1,000 per day and possible revocation.

The host also needs a Transient Room Tax permit from the city Finance Department and a license from Public Health Madison and Dane County, and the ZTRHP permit is withheld until both exist. Before you list, ask Building Inspection to confirm your permit status in writing.

A sale does not move tenants out, so the buyer gets the lease along with the maintenance record. Tenants can complain to Madison Building Inspection when a housing provider is slow with repairs, and a complaint on file may come up in a buyer's questions. Finish open repairs first and keep the receipts together.

Check the lease end date and notice terms before you promise anyone a closing date. A vacant unit at closing means planning around the lease and the state landlord-tenant rules that the Department of Agriculture, Trade and Consumer Protection publishes and the city links for owners.

Madison's assessor sets values as of January 1, and the challenge process happens in spring and summer. Notices go out near the start of May, followed by an Open Book window in early May. Objections to the Board of Assessors are due by mid-May, and the Assessor's Office posts exact dates each year. The Board of Review is the last municipal step.

Use Open Book to fix facts like room counts or a permit that was unfinished on January 1. When the facts are right but the number is wrong, file an objection with the Board of Assessors. The office takes calls at 608-266-4531 and email at openbook@cityofmadison.com. Commercial and multi-unit owners must add income and expense information to an objection.

sections.h2: Wisconsin rules for a Madison seller
sections.html:
Almost every sale triggers two state rules. Wis. Stat. 77.22 puts a transfer fee of 30 cents per $100 of value on the seller, and Wis. Stat. 709.02 makes the seller of a one-to-four unit property furnish a condition report.

  • Deliver the condition report within 10 days of acceptance. If the buyer never gets it, they may rescind in the 2 business days after the 10-day period ends.
  • A fiduciary appointed by a court who never lived there need not file the report.
  • The Department of Revenue's exemptions include transfers by will or descent, foreclosure deeds to the lender and transfers between spouses.
  • Reporting a false or understated value can draw a penalty of $25 or 25% of the added fee, whichever is greater.

Even an as-is cash buyer receives the report, and the return still gets filed.

A few items are worth settling before the closing date arrives.

  • Confirm the permit history with Building Inspection, including anything left open.
  • Collect the lease, repair receipts and any complaint records if the house is rented.
  • Deliver the condition report on time and keep proof of when it went out.
  • Have the return completed and the receipt ready for the deed package.
  • Ask for tax and payoff figures so the closing agent can prepare a settlement statement.

Cash buyers go through the same list, though without a lender's appraisal and underwriting the calendar is shorter.

sections.h2: Recording the deed in Dane County
sections.html:
Recording at the Dane County Register of Deeds costs $30 per document and requires an Electronic Transfer Return receipt. The deed names grantor and grantee, bears the grantor's notarized signature, gives the legal description and the tax bill's parcel number, and shows a return address. Only the original with original signatures is accepted. Photocopies are refused.

Mailing is possible: send the package to PO Box 1438, Madison, WI 53701-1438, with the recording fee and any transfer fee combined on a single check. Questions go to (608) 266-4141. An attorney or title company usually drafts the deed, because the office cannot complete one for you.

faqs.q: Can I rent my Madison house short term without a permit?
faqs.a: No. A ZTRHP permit comes first, and the house must be your primary dwelling. A Transient Room Tax permit and a Public Health license are also required, along with a $300 application fee and $100 a year to renew.

faqs.q: Will the buyer get my short-term rental permit in Madison?
faqs.a: No. It belongs to a specific host and unit and cannot be transferred. A buyer who wants to host guests applies separately and must meet the primary-dwelling rule.

faqs.q: Who covers the transfer fee on a Madison sale?
faqs.a: The seller. Wis. Stat. 77.22 sets 30 cents per $100 of value, collected at recording. Transfers by will or between spouses are among the exemptions.

faqs.q: When must the Madison buyer get the condition report?
faqs.a: Within 10 days after the contract is accepted. A late report gives the buyer 2 business days after that period to rescind and recover deposits under Wis. Stat. 709.02.

faqs.q: Where is a Madison deed recorded?
faqs.a: At the Dane County Register of Deeds, which charges $30 per document and needs the Electronic Transfer Return receipt. The mailing address is PO Box 1438, Madison, WI 53701-1438.
